title: "How the fees are measured"
description: "Why the real Amazon cut is not the one on the fee schedule."
---

<!-- Generated by scripts/sync-docs.mjs from ciyalabs/biryar.
     Edit the document in that repository, not this file. -->

Most sellers work out their profit from the percentage on Amazon's fee
table. Biryar does not. It reads what Amazon actually kept from your own
sales, and on cheap products that is a very different number.

This page shows why, with arithmetic you can check on paper. The figures
in the examples are invented and chosen to be round. Your own figures come
out of your own account.

## The short version

Amazon's fee table states a percentage: 15% for many categories, which
is 17.85% once German VAT on the fee is added. That is not what Amazon
takes. On a cheap product, measured from real payouts, the cut is
**between 33% and 43% of the sale price**.

Nothing is hidden and nothing is wrong. The difference is made of charges
that are not percentages:

- a fixed fee per item sold, the same whether the item costs €3 or €300,
- the postage label, bought through Amazon and charged to the order,
- fulfilment charges that depend on the unit and not on its price,
- VAT on those fees.

A fixed charge is a large part of a small sale and a small part of a large
one. A percentage cannot say that.

## The arithmetic

Amazon's cut on one unit has two parts: a percentage of the price, and a
fixed amount.

```
Amazon's cut = rate × price + fixed charge
```

As a share of the price, which is how a seller thinks of it:

```
share = rate + fixed charge ÷ price
```

The second part is the whole story. It gets smaller as the price goes up,
because the same fixed charge is spread over a bigger sale. So "Amazon
takes about so many per cent" is not a fact about Amazon or about a
category. It is a fact about **the price of the thing you sold**.

With a rate of 17.85% and a fixed charge of €1.00, and nothing changing
except the price:

| Sale price | Amazon takes | As a share |
|---|---|---|
| €3.00 | €1.54 | **51.2%** |
| €5.00 | €1.89 | **37.9%** |
| €10.00 | €2.79 | 27.9% |
| €15.00 | €3.68 | 24.5% |
| €30.00 | €6.35 | 21.2% |
| €50.00 | €9.92 | 19.8% |

Two things to take from this. The share comes down towards the rate and
never reaches it, so the fee table's percentage is the least Amazon takes,
not an estimate of what it takes. And on a cheap product the gap is not a
rounding error: at €5 the real cut is more than twice the rate.

## Why this matters for a price floor

The floor is the lowest price at which a sale does not lose money. A floor
worked out from the percentage alone is too low, so a repricer using it
will happily sell at a loss and report a profit while doing it.

Measured properly, the floor is:

```
break-even price = (what the unit cost you + fixed charge) ÷ (1 − rate)
```

Continuing the example, for a unit that cost you €3.00:

| | |
|---|---|
| The floor with both parts, `(3.00 + 1.00) ÷ (1 − 0.1785)` | **€4.87** |
| At €4.87, what reaches you | €3.00, exactly the cost |
| The floor from the percentage alone, `3.00 ÷ (1 − 0.1785)` | **€3.65** |
| At €3.65, what reaches you | €2.00 |
| Loss on every unit | **€1.00** |

The loss is exactly the fixed charge. That is the useful part: **a floor
that leaves out the fixed charge is wrong by the fixed charge, on every
unit, every time.**

This is the floor Biryar's repricer uses, with the rate and the fixed
charge measured from your own sales. See [Repricing](/guide/repricing/).

## Why Biryar will not work out your cost for you

The same formula can be turned around to get a cost from a price:

```
cost = price × (1 − rate) − fixed charge
```

It is tempting to use that to fill in a missing buy price from a price
floor in Seller Central. Biryar does not, because the result proves
nothing. A cost worked out from a floor gives back the same floor when it
is put through the formula again, whether the cost is right or nonsense. A
check that cannot fail is not a check.

What you paid for a unit is the one number Amazon never reports, and every
profit figure depends on it. The only thing that can confirm it is a
supplier's invoice, with a quantity and a printed price. So Biryar takes
your costs from your invoices, or from what you type in, and leaves profit
blank where it has none. See [Portfolio](/guide/portfolio/).

## Where your own figures come from

Biryar reads the record of every sale Amazon has paid out to you: what the
buyer paid, each fee, the postage. From those it works out your own rate
and your own fixed charge, and uses that pair everywhere: for the profit
on a product, for the floor under a price, and for deciding whether a
deal in a shop would make money.

One paid-out sale is enough to start, and the figures get steadier as more
sales arrive.
